title: Chapter 32 — Browser to Buyer: Capture and Conversion
intro: Customers no longer distinguish between online and in-store. Neither should you. The channel changes. The selling does not. This chapter teaches you how to sell from wherever the customer is.

sections.title: Every Channel Is a Showroom
sections.content:
Whether a customer walks through the front door, starts a live chat, sends a Facebook message, texts, emails, or joins a video call — the sales process remains the same.

The channel changes. The selling does not.

This is one of the most important ideas in this entire program. Most retailers treat live chat as a lead generation tool. Customer comes in online, someone engages them, and they try to set up an appointment in store. That treats the online customer as a future opportunity.

That is the wrong approach.

Treat them as today's customer. The objective should not be 'come into the store.' The objective should be 'how can I help you buy today?'

Every conversation should be treated as a complete sales opportunity — all 10 Steps of Selling, from engagement through follow-up, regardless of channel.

sections.title: Stop Generating Leads — Start Generating Sales
sections.content:
The internet has become the first showroom. Customers now arrive having already compared prices, watched YouTube reviews, read owner reviews, compared brands, explored specifications, viewed photos, and used 3D product viewers.

They have done work. Respect that work.

The salesperson should continue the customer's journey — not restart it. When someone reaches out online and you ask them the same questions they already answered on your website, you are telling them their time did not matter.

Instead, ask what they have found so far. Ask what brought them to you specifically. Ask where they are in their decision. Then pick up the 10 Steps from wherever they already are. Some online customers are at Step 3 — discovery. Others are at Step 8 — they just need their last objection handled. Meet them where they are.

sections.title: Live Chat Is Selling
sections.content:
Live chat should follow exactly the same framework as showroom selling.

Step 1 — Engagement. Step 2 — Rapport. Step 3 — Discovery. Step 4 — Needs Assessment. Step 5 — Wants Assessment. Step 6 — Product Recommendation. Step 7 — Presentation. Step 8 — Objection Handling. Step 9 — Closing. Step 10 — Follow-up.

Only the communication channel changes. The words are different — you are typing instead of talking. The pace is different — they may respond in 30 seconds or 5 minutes. But the structure is identical.

The reason this is not adopted as thoroughly as it should be is simple: we are used to selling how we sell. Customer comes in from an ad, customer walks the floor, we do our demo. But customers have access to so much information now that many of them are prepared to buy online. When you look at the sales of Amazon, Best Buy, Walmart — these companies are investing billions in their online presence. Customers want to buy here, now, today. If your store does not give them that capability, someone else will.

sections.title: When Words Are Not Enough — Bring the Showroom to Them
sections.content:
Some products need to be experienced. Instead of asking the customer to drive to the store, bring the showroom to them.

The easiest way to do a proper product demonstration online is to convert to a video call. If your system does not have it, there are many ways: Google Meet, Zoom, Microsoft Teams, FaceTime, WhatsApp. The only thing you need is your cell phone.

Customer is sitting at home and says they want to see the product. Set up a call. Take your phone. Walk over to the product. Do the same product demonstration that you would do in store. Do not alter it. Do not get awkward because it is a video. Show them the product with your camera while speaking to them. You can even step back a little and do your same demonstration with you in the video.

Why is this a benefit? Because a lot of times multiple decision-makers need to agree, and you only have one of them in front of you. If both are on the video call and you do this presentation, you are cutting out the 'I will be back with my partner' conversation entirely.

sections.title: The Scout Problem — Solved
sections.content:
Many purchases involve more than one decision-maker. Often one person gathers information — I call them the Scout — while another approves the purchase.

Traditional retail creates friction with this. 'I will come back with my spouse.' 'We will think about it.' 'I will show them later.' Every one of those is a lost sale waiting to happen.

Modern technology removes that friction. If the second decision-maker is unavailable, invite them into the video call. FaceTime, WhatsApp, Google Meet, Teams — whatever works for the customer.

Allow everyone to experience the presentation together. Questions are answered immediately. Objections are handled together. Confidence increases. The buying journey becomes shorter and more collaborative.

Today's software gives us the opportunity to change how we sell and deliver presentations that not everybody is doing. That is your edge.

sections.title: Convenience Is Value
sections.content:
Customers are busy. Many have children, demanding careers, long commutes, elderly parents, limited free time. Reducing effort is part of customer service.

If technology eliminates an unnecessary trip to the store, use it. If a video call at 8pm after the kids are in bed closes the deal, do it. Convenience has become a competitive advantage.

The question you should always ask yourself: 'What is the easiest way for this customer to buy confidently?' Sometimes that means coming into the showroom. Sometimes it means staying at home. The best solution depends on the customer — not on your habits.

Customers do not wake up wanting to visit a showroom. They wake up wanting to solve a problem. If you can solve that problem professionally from wherever they are, you have delivered a better experience than simply asking them to drive to your store.

sections.title: Coaching Rule
sections.content:
When evaluating online and omnichannel selling, ask:

Was the online customer treated like a real customer or merely a lead to convert to an in-store visit?
Was the full 10-step process followed — discovery, needs, wants, recommendation, presentation — or was it just 'come visit us'?
Was a video demonstration offered when appropriate?
Were all decision-makers included whenever possible?
Was unnecessary effort removed from the customer's buying journey?
Did the salesperson adapt the process to the customer's preferred channel?

Do not sell the store. Sell the customer. Meet them where they are. Sell the way they want to buy.
